questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: The judge explains the reasons for a decree. What is this statement called?
questions.why: A judgment gives the reasons. A decree formally records the determination of rights. The two belong together but are different documents.
questions.scenario: The court says why Ayesha succeeds, explaining the factual and legal reasons. Which document supplies those reasons?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which description best fits a decree?
questions.answer: Formal adjudication conclusively determining rights in the suit
questions.why: A decree determines rights in controversy and may be preliminary or final. An ordinary procedural order does not automatically become a decree.
questions.scenario: A court formally settles the parties' rights over disputed land. Which CPC term fits that formal determination?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which is included in the CPC definition of a decree?
questions.why: Rejection of a plaint is expressly included. Dismissal for default is expressly excluded. This distinction affects the available remedy.
questions.scenario: Two outcomes occur: one plaint is rejected; another suit is dismissed because nobody attends. Which outcome counts as a decree under the definition?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: In the CPC definition, Code includes what?
questions.why: The definition brings the procedural rules within the Code. Do not treat the First Schedule as a separate unrelated law.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Who is a decree-holder?
questions.answer: A person with a decree or executable order in their favour
wrong: Only the person who first filed the suit
questions.why: The definition follows the benefit of the decree or executable order. A defendant can also obtain a decree in their favour.
questions.scenario: Bilal wins an executable order even though Ayesha originally filed the suit. What does Bilal become?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: An executable order is made against Bilal. What is his CPC description?
questions.why: The judgment-debtor is the person against whom a decree or executable order is made. It does not mean every person accused of owing money.
questions.scenario: A decree orders Ayesha to pay Bilal. What is Ayesha's description under the CPC?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Civil courts generally try civil suits except those whose cognizance is what?
questions.why: Section 9 begins with general civil jurisdiction, then recognises legal bars. A defendant's objection alone does not remove jurisdiction.
questions.cue: Civil suits enter unless law bars them.
questions.scenario: Bilal says the civil court cannot hear a case merely because he objects. What kind of bar is actually recognised by section 9?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: The same substantial issue is already in a previously instituted qualifying suit. Which provision concerns staying the later trial?
questions.why: Section 10 concerns a pending earlier suit, subject to its party and jurisdiction conditions. It stays trial; it does not decide the merits.
questions.scenario: The earlier suit is still pending and the statutory identity requirements are met. Which section addresses stopping the later trial?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A competent court has already finally decided the same issue between the relevant parties. Which principle may bar trying it again?
questions.why: Section 11 deals with an issue already heard and finally decided, with the statutory identity requirements. Pending litigation is section 10.
questions.scenario: Ayesha wants to retry an issue finally decided by a competent court between the relevant parties. Which principle is the obstacle?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A ground might and ought to have been raised in the former suit. Which provision treats it as directly and substantially in issue?
questions.why: Constructive res judicata prevents a party withholding a necessary ground and starting another round of litigation about it.
questions.cue: Might + ought = should have raised it.
questions.scenario: Bilal saves a ground that he could and should have raised, hoping to litigate it later. Which provision addresses that tactic?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A person challenges a final judgment for fraud, misrepresentation or want of jurisdiction. Section 12(2) directs an application to whom?
questions.answer: The court that passed the final judgment, decree or order
wrong: Any court chosen by the applicant
questions.why: The specified remedy is an application to the court that passed the final decision, rather than a separate suit on these grounds.
questions.scenario: Ayesha alleges that the final decree was obtained by fraud. Where does section 12(2) direct her application?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Where should a suit ordinarily be instituted under section 15?
questions.answer: The court of the lowest grade competent to try it
questions.why: Both grade and competence matter. A lower court without the required jurisdiction does not become competent merely because it is lower.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Subject to statutory qualifications, a suit for partition of land belongs where?
questions.why: Section 16 connects specified property suits with the property's location, subject to jurisdictional limits and its proviso.
questions.scenario: A partition dispute concerns a plot in Lahore. Subject to the Code's qualifications, which location connects the suit to its court?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Land lies within two court jurisdictions. Under section 17, where may a qualifying suit be brought?
questions.answer: A competent court where any part is situated
wrong: Both courts in separate identical suits
questions.why: A court with part of the property in its area may hear it if the entire claim falls within its pecuniary competence.
questions.cue: Any part; competence for the whole claim.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A wrong occurs in Quetta; the defendant resides in Karachi. Under section 19, the plaintiff may ordinarily choose which forum?
questions.answer: Either the place of wrong or defendant's residence
questions.why: For compensation for wrong to a person or movable property, section 19 offers the specified alternatives to the plaintiff.
questions.scenario: Bilal lives in Karachi but the alleged personal wrong occurred in Quetta. What choice does section 19 generally give Ayesha?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Section 20 links other suits to the defendant's location or what?
questions.answer: Where the cause of action arises wholly or partly
wrong: Where a newspaper is printed in every case
questions.why: A material part of the cause of action may support territorial jurisdiction. The plaintiff's convenience alone is insufficient.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Questions between the suit's parties about execution, discharge or satisfaction are normally decided by whom?
wrong: A new court through a separate suit
questions.why: Section 47 directs these questions to the court executing the decree and avoids a separate suit about them.
questions.scenario: The parties disagree about whether a decree has been satisfied. Who should ordinarily resolve this rather than a fresh suit?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which is a purpose for which a civil court may issue a commission under section 75?
questions.why: Commissions can assist with examination, local investigation, accounts and partition. The court retains the judicial decision.
questions.scenario: The judge needs someone to inspect the disputed location and report. Which commission purpose fits?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Subject to the Code and other applicable law, section 96 concerns appeals from what?
questions.why: Section 96 provides the general route of appeal from an original decree. Exceptions still matter, including consent decrees.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Does section 96 permit an appeal from an original decree passed ex parte?
questions.why: Section 96(2) expressly allows it. Order IX rule 13 supplies a different remedy to set aside an ex parte decree on its own grounds.
questions.cue: Ex parte does not erase appeal.
questions.scenario: A decree is entered while Bilal is absent. Is an appeal from an original ex parte decree permitted by section 96(2)?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Under section 96(3), is an appeal available from a decree passed with the parties' consent?
wrong: Only because one party changed their mind
questions.why: A consent decree is excluded from this appeal route. A distinct allegation such as fraud raises different questions and remedies.
questions.cue: Consent closes the ordinary appeal route.
questions.scenario: Both parties consent to a decree, then one merely changes their mind. Is the ordinary section 96 appeal available?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which section identifies orders from which appeals lie?
questions.why: Appeals from orders require a statutory basis. Section 104 and Order XLIII should be learned together.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Section 115 principally addresses what kind of defect in a qualifying decided case?
questions.answer: Jurisdictional error or illegal/materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction
questions.why: Revision is not a second ordinary appeal. The listed jurisdictional conditions and absence of an appeal to the High Court matter.
questions.scenario: A subordinate court failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it, and the other statutory requirements are met. What kind of problem does revision address?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which section preserves orders needed for justice or prevention of abuse of process?
questions.why: Section 151 saves inherent powers. It is not permission to ignore an express rule of the Code.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Order I primarily deals with what?
questions.why: Think first about who belongs in the case. Joinder provisions concern plaintiffs and defendants and the conditions for including them.
questions.scenario: Ayesha needs to decide whom to join as a defendant. Which Order should she open first?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Under Order VI rule 1, pleading means what?
questions.why: The plaintiff's plaint and defendant's written statement set out the competing cases. Evidence proves those cases later.
questions.scenario: Ayesha files her claim and Bilal files his defence. What collective label covers those two papers?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: What should pleadings state under Order VI rule 2?
questions.answer: Material facts relied on, rather than the evidence proving them
questions.why: State the essential facts needed for the claim or defence. Do not confuse the facts to be proved with the evidence used to prove them.
questions.scenario: Ayesha is drafting her plaint. Should she narrate every witness's testimony or identify the essential facts?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which rule generally concerns alteration or amendment of pleadings?
questions.why: Amendment may help determine the real questions in controversy, subject to the court's conditions and applicable law.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which Order primarily sets out rules about the plaint?
questions.why: The plaint presents the plaintiff's claim. It includes essential particulars, and the Order also addresses return and rejection.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: The plaint belongs before a different court. Which rule deals with returning it for proper presentation?
questions.why: Return addresses the proper court for institution. Rejection under rule 11 concerns specified defects or legal bars.
questions.scenario: The judge says this claim should have been presented in another competent court. Which rule concerns returning the plaint?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A plaint discloses no cause of action. Which rule provides for rejection?
questions.why: Failure to disclose a cause of action is a listed rejection ground. Merely losing on evidence at trial is a different situation.
questions.scenario: Even accepting its assertions, the plaint discloses no cause of action. Which rule supplies the rejection ground?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which Order principally concerns the written statement and set-off?
questions.why: This is the defendant's response. Connect the sequence: VI general pleadings, VII plaint, VIII defence.

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: A defendant says only 'everything is denied'. What does Order VIII require instead?
questions.answer: Specific and non-evasive answers to allegations of fact
questions.why: Rules 3 and 4 require specific denials addressing the substance. A vague blanket denial is not a safe substitute.
questions.scenario: Bilal's defence says only 'I deny everything'. What type of response do the pleading rules require?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: For the legal set-off described in Order VIII rule 6, the money claimed must be what?
questions.answer: An ascertained sum legally recoverable, with the rule's other conditions
questions.why: The rule concerns an ascertained monetary cross-demand and includes capacity and jurisdiction conditions. Unassessed damages do not meet that basic requirement.
questions.scenario: Bilal wants to set off an unassessed claim for damages. What feature required for legal set-off is missing?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Under Order IX rule 3, what may the court do if neither party appears?
questions.why: This is dismissal for default, not a decision proving the claim false on its merits. Restoration provisions should be considered separately.
questions.cue: No one appears: suit may go.
questions.scenario: Neither Ayesha nor Bilal comes when their suit is called. What may the court order under Order IX rule 3?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Plaintiff appears, defendant does not, and summons was duly served. What may the court do?
wrong: Automatically award every amount claimed without proof
questions.why: The court may proceed without the defendant under Order IX. The plaintiff still has to establish the case as required.
questions.cue: Absent after due service = ex parte.
questions.scenario: Ayesha attends. Bilal, duly served, does not. How may the court proceed?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which provision addresses setting aside an ex parte decree for non-service or sufficient cause preventing appearance?
questions.why: Apply to the court that passed the decree. The rule's grounds and applicable conditions must be established.
questions.scenario: Bilal shows sufficient cause that prevented his attendance when the decree was passed ex parte. Which provision supplies the set-aside route?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Which Order concerns temporary injunctions and interlocutory orders?
questions.why: An injunction can preserve the position pending adjudication. It is not itself the final determination of all rights.
questions.scenario: Ayesha wants temporary protection while a civil dispute is decided. Which Order concerns that relief?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: Does merely filing an appeal automatically stay execution of a decree?
wrong: Only if the appeal is handwritten
Only if counsel requests orally outside court
questions.why: Order XLI rule 5 says an appeal does not by itself operate as a stay. A stay order must be obtained on the applicable grounds.
questions.cue: Appeal filed is not stay granted.
questions.scenario: Bilal files an appeal and assumes execution has stopped automatically. Is that assumption correct?

questions.subject: CPC
questions.q: What form does an appeal under Order XLI rule 1 take?
questions.answer: A memorandum signed by appellant or pleader
wrong: A fresh plaint in every case
questions.why: The memorandum sets out grounds of appeal. Order XLI addresses appeals from original decrees; XLIII addresses appeals from orders.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Which proceeding is excluded from QSO's general application clause?
questions.why: Article 1 applies broadly to judicial proceedings, including courts martial and tribunals, but expressly excludes proceedings before an arbitrator.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Can a person's intention or state of mind count as a fact under QSO?
wrong: Only a confession is a fact
questions.why: The definition includes mental conditions of which a person is conscious. A fact need not be something you can touch.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A fact is neither proved nor disproved. What is its classification?
questions.why: Not proved means the evidence has established neither existence nor non-existence to the required standard. It is not the same as disproved.
questions.scenario: After hearing both sides, the court is satisfied neither that a fact exists nor that it does not. How is it classified?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Witness statements permitted or required by the court about facts under inquiry are what?
questions.why: QSO distinguishes witness statements from documents produced for inspection. Both may count as evidence through different routes.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Does young age alone automatically make a witness incompetent?
questions.answer: No; understanding questions and giving rational answers matters
wrong: Only if the witness owns property
questions.why: Article 3 uses a functional test, including whether age or another condition prevents understanding or rational answers.
questions.scenario: A child understands the questions and can answer rationally. Does age alone automatically exclude the testimony?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: What does Article 5 principally protect, subject to its exceptions?
wrong: All facts ever seen by a married person
questions.why: Communications made during marriage are protected even after the marriage ends. The maker or representative may consent. Exceptions include suits between spouses and prosecution of one for a crime against the other.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: What is the general rule about an advocate disclosing protected client communications?
questions.answer: Disclosure is restricted without express client consent, subject to exceptions
wrong: Privilege ends automatically when the case ends
questions.why: Article 9 protects professional communications but excludes, for example, communications furthering an illegal purpose. The obligation continues after employment ends.
questions.cue: Legal advice is confidential, not a shield for illegality.
questions.scenario: A former client ends the retainer. Does that alone allow disclosure of protected communications? Choose the general rule.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Under Article 16, is an accomplice generally a competent witness, apart from its stated hadd exception?
wrong: Only if a judge becomes counsel
questions.why: Competence is distinct from the caution about corroboration. Do not confuse 'can testify' with 'must automatically be believed'.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Which Article permits evidence of facts in issue and legally relevant facts?
questions.why: Relevance has to come through QSO. A fact being interesting or prejudicial does not by itself make it legally relevant.
questions.scenario: Ayesha wants to present an interesting but legally unrelated rumour. Which Article limits evidence to facts in issue and relevant facts?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Facts so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction are addressed by which Article?
questions.why: The connection is transactional, not merely that two events occurred on the same day. This is commonly studied as res gestae.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Which Article concerns motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct?
questions.why: Motive can explain why; preparation can show planning; conduct may illuminate events. They remain subject to the Article's conditions.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Facts necessary to explain or introduce a relevant fact, including identity where relevant, fall under which Article?
questions.why: Context and identification can make other evidence understandable. Article 22 is broader than simply naming a person.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A statement suggesting an inference about a fact in issue or relevant fact is generally called what?
questions.why: Article 30 defines admissions. Whether a statement is an admission and against whom it is provable depends on the following Articles.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Which is the safer distinction?
questions.answer: An admission is broader; a confession concerns acknowledgment of guilt
wrong: Every admission is necessarily a full confession
Admissions occur only in criminal trials
questions.why: A person may admit one fact without confessing the offence. Avoid treating an isolated incriminating fact as automatically a complete confession.
questions.scenario: Bilal admits he was at the location but denies committing the offence. Which statement best explains why that is not automatically a confession?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A qualifying inducement, threat or promise from a person in authority can make a confession what?
questions.answer: Irrelevant in criminal proceedings under Article 37
questions.why: Article 37 protects against confessions affected by the specified improper inducement, threat or promise. Its conditions must be satisfied.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: What is the general rule under Article 38?
questions.answer: A confession to a police officer cannot be proved against the accused
wrong: Only written police confessions are allowed
A constable can waive the rule
questions.why: The prohibition concerns confession to a police officer. Discovery information has a limited separate rule in Article 40.
questions.scenario: An accused confesses to a police officer. Which statement gives Article 38's general rule?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Under Article 39, a confession in police custody is generally excluded unless made in whose immediate presence?
questions.why: The rule concerns custody even where the statement is made to someone other than police. Article 40 separately addresses discovery.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Police discover an object from information supplied by an accused in custody. How much information may Article 40 permit to be proved?
questions.answer: Only the portion distinctly relating to the discovered fact
questions.why: Discovery is a limited exception. It does not make the whole confession admissible merely because one item was found.
questions.scenario: An accused's statement leads police to an object, but also contains a long confession. How much does the discovery rule potentially admit?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Does a qualifying statement about the cause of death require the maker to have expected death?
questions.why: Article 46(1) does not require expectation of death. The cause of the maker's death must come into question and other requirements apply.
questions.cue: Cause of death, not expectation of death.
questions.scenario: A person describes the cause of an injury, expecting recovery, but later dies. Must expectation of death have existed for Article 46(1)?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Opinions of persons specially skilled in relevant fields are addressed by which Article?
questions.why: Experts assist on the matters specified, such as science, art and handwriting. Their opinion does not automatically bind the court.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Is character generally relevant simply to prove conduct imputed in a civil case?
questions.answer: No, subject to the Article's qualification
questions.why: Article 66 generally excludes this use, while character may emerge from otherwise relevant facts. Damage-related character is a separate rule.
questions.cue: Civil conduct is not proved by reputation alone.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: In criminal proceedings, is the accused's previous good character relevant?
wrong: Only if a police officer approves
questions.why: Article 67 permits previous good character. It does not guarantee acquittal; all evidence still has to be assessed.
questions.cue: Good character may help, not decide.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: If evidence concerns something that could be seen, the witness should ordinarily be someone who did what?
questions.why: Article 71 generally requires direct oral evidence: the witness must have the corresponding personal perception.
questions.cue: Seen by me, not told to me.
questions.scenario: A witness says, 'My neighbour told me she saw it.' If the fact could be seen, whose perception does Article 71 ordinarily require?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Document contents may be proved through which categories?
questions.why: Article 72 introduces primary and secondary evidence. Secondary evidence is not freely interchangeable with an available original; Article 76 gives conditions.
questions.cue: Documents: original route or permitted substitute.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: What is the basic definition of primary evidence?
questions.answer: The document itself produced for court inspection
questions.why: Article 73 starts with the document itself. Its explanations deal with counterparts and other situations, so 'only one possible original' is too simple.
questions.scenario: Ayesha brings the actual signed document for the court to inspect. Which basic evidence category is this?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Which is a recognised type of secondary evidence, subject to admissibility conditions?
questions.answer: A certified copy given under law
questions.why: Article 74 lists types of secondary evidence; Article 76 governs when secondary evidence of contents may be given.
questions.cue: A copy needs a legal route.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Records of acts of public officers are classified under which Article?
questions.why: Article 85 identifies public documents. Article 86 says other documents are private; proof rules then differ.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Must a fact judicially noticeable be proved by ordinary evidence?
questions.why: Article 111 dispenses with proof of facts of which judicial notice is taken. Article 112 lists matters for judicial notice.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Do facts admitted in the ways specified by Article 113 normally need proof?
questions.answer: No, but the court may require proof
questions.why: The court retains discretion to demand proof despite an admission. The 2025 amendment corrects 'rule or pleading' to 'rule of pleading'.
questions.cue: Admission can save proof; court keeps discretion.
questions.scenario: The parties admit a fact in the required manner. What is the normal proof position, including the court's discretion?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A person intentionally causes another to believe and act on a fact. What may prevent later denial in the relevant proceedings?
questions.why: Article 114 addresses representation and reliance. It is not simply a penalty for changing an opinion.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Who normally proves facts asserted to obtain a judgment on a claimed right or liability?
questions.why: Article 117 links the burden to the facts a person asks the court to rely on. The burden may differ for distinct issues.
questions.cue: You assert the necessary fact; you prove it.
questions.scenario: Ayesha says a will gives her the land and asks the court for possession. Who normally proves the necessary facts she asserts?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Article 118 places the burden on whom if neither side gave evidence?
wrong: Always the plaintiff regardless of issue
questions.why: Ask who loses if the record remains empty. This is a practical way to identify the burden in the particular proceeding.
questions.cue: Who loses on an empty record?
questions.scenario: Imagine neither side produces any evidence. Which party does Article 118 use to identify the burden?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A fact is especially within a person's knowledge. Article 122 generally places its burden on whom?
questions.why: This rule concerns specially known facts. It does not erase the prosecution's overall responsibility to establish an offence.
questions.cue: Your special knowledge, your proof of that fact.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: A person is shown to have been alive within thirty years. Who bears the burden of proving death?
questions.why: Article 123 supplies this allocation, subject to Article 124's special seven-year rule. Do not swap the two periods.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.topic: Not heard of for seven years
questions.q: A person has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally hear. Who must prove the person is alive?
questions.why: Article 124 changes the burden concerning life. It does not automatically establish a precise date or time of death.
questions.cue: Seven years: burden shifts, date does not appear.
questions.scenario: The natural contacts of a missing person have heard nothing for seven years. Who bears the burden of showing the person is alive?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: The adverse party questions a witness. What is this called?
questions.why: The party calling the witness conducts examination-in-chief; the opponent cross-examines; the calling party may then re-examine.
questions.cue: Own side, other side, own side again.
questions.scenario: Bilal's advocate questions Ayesha's witness. What is that stage called?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Questions suggesting the desired answer are generally allowed in which examination?
questions.why: Articles 136-138 distinguish the definition and permitted use. In chief or re-examination, objection and court permission matter.
questions.scenario: An advocate asks, 'You were at the gate at 9 pm, weren't you?' In which stage are leading questions generally permitted?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Before proving a contradictory written statement, what must be drawn to the witness's attention?
questions.answer: The relevant parts intended for contradiction
questions.why: Article 140 requires attention to the specific parts relied on when contradiction is intended. A vague allegation is not enough.
questions.scenario: Counsel intends to contradict a witness using an old written account. What part of the procedure must happen before proving the contradiction?

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Who may permit the party calling a witness to ask questions ordinarily put in cross-examination?
questions.why: Article 150 gives the court discretion. A party cannot assume automatic permission merely by calling a witness hostile.
questions.cue: Court permits cross of your own witness.

questions.subject: QSO
questions.q: Article 164 permits the court to consider evidence made available through what?
questions.why: Electronic or scientific material can be produced through this provision, but reliability and proof still matter. Technology does not make evidence automatically true.
questions.scenario: A party has a recording made by a modern device. Which type of evidence does Article 164 potentially permit, subject to proper proof?

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In the constitutional Preamble, sovereignty over the entire universe belongs to whom?
questions.why: The Preamble places sovereignty with Almighty Allah and describes authority exercised by Pakistan's people through prescribed limits as a sacred trust.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article makes the Objectives Resolution a substantive part of the Constitution?
questions.why: The letter A matters: Article 2 concerns Islam as the State religion; Article 2A concerns the Objectives Resolution.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Under Article 8, a law inconsistent with fundamental rights is void to what extent?
questions.answer: To the extent of the inconsistency
wrong: The whole legal system becomes void
questions.why: The phrase limits invalidity to the inconsistent part, subject to Article 8's own provisions. It does not automatically erase every part of every law.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article protects life and liberty except in accordance with law?
questions.why: Article 9 protects security of person. Distinguish it from the procedural guarantees of fair trial in Article 10A.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: A person's civil rights or a criminal charge are being determined. Which Article expressly provides fair trial and due process?
questions.why: Article 10A applies to determination of civil rights and obligations as well as criminal charges. It is not confined to criminal trials.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article protects dignity and, subject to law, privacy of the home?
questions.why: Article 14 also prohibits torture for extracting evidence. Link dignity with the home and protection from coercive evidence extraction.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Freedom of speech and expression, subject to listed reasonable restrictions, is under which Article?
questions.why: The right is constitutionally protected but not unlimited. Article 19A is a separate right to information.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article grants citizens access to information in matters of public importance, subject to law?
questions.why: The right has its own provision and qualifications. Do not swap it with speech under Article 19.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Equality before law and equal protection of law are principally in which Article?
questions.why: Article 25 is the general equality provision. Other Articles address specific contexts such as public places and public employment.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Article 25A provides free and compulsory education for which ages?
questions.why: The exact constitutional range is five to sixteen, in the manner determined by law. Do not import age limits from another jurisdiction.
questions.scenario: You see an education question offering 5-16, 5-18, 6-14 and 7-21. Which range does Article 25A use?

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Majlis-e-Shoora consists of which three components?
questions.why: Article 50 includes the President even though the President is not a chamber. Pakistan has two parliamentary Houses.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Unless sooner dissolved, the National Assembly's term is how long from its first meeting?
questions.why: The starting point is its first meeting, not election day. Earlier dissolution is expressly possible.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which statement about the Senate is correct?
questions.answer: It is not subject to dissolution
wrong: It dissolves with every National Assembly
It is elected for one year
It is dissolved by every budget
questions.why: The Senate is a continuing House with staggered terms. Avoid confusing its members' terms with the life of the House.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: What minimum age does Article 62 prescribe for National Assembly membership?
questions.why: Twenty-five concerns the National Assembly; the Senate's age qualification is thirty. Other qualifications also apply.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Without leave, absence for how many consecutive days of a House's sittings may lead the House to declare a seat vacant?
questions.why: Count consecutive sitting days under Article 64(2), not simply forty calendar days on holiday.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: A Money Bill originates in which House?
questions.why: Article 73 gives the National Assembly the originating role. The Senate has a recommendation role under the constitutional procedure.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Under the Constitution updated to 21 November 2025, which court has exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes between two or more Governments?
wrong: Supreme Court under the former Article 184
questions.why: Article 175E now provides this jurisdiction. Article 184 was omitted by the Twenty-seventh Amendment. Older sample papers need their historical date kept visible.
questions.scenario: An old sample says Supreme Court and Article 184. A question instead expressly asks for the position in the November 2025 Constitution. Which court now hears inter-government disputes?

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Under amended Article 189, which court's legal decisions bind all other courts including the Supreme Court?
questions.why: The updated Article distinguishes FCC decisions from Supreme Court decisions, which bind other courts except the FCC.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: In the Constitution updated to 21 November 2025, the minimum age for a High Court judge is what?
questions.why: Article 193(2) now states forty, together with citizenship and experience requirements. The older forty-five-year answer should not be used as current law.

questions.subject: Constitution
questions.q: Which Article principally sets out the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction?
questions.why: Article 199 addresses specified orders and jurisdictional conditions. Read it with applicable constitutional-bench provisions rather than assuming old institutional arrangements.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Rule 134 requires an advocate to uphold what?
questions.answer: Professional dignity and their own standing
wrong: Only the number of cases won
questions.why: The duty concerns the profession and the individual advocate. Winning does not justify conduct that damages either.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: What is the general rule about soliciting professional employment by advertisement?
questions.answer: It is prohibited, with limited ordinary-listing exceptions
wrong: Only judges may advertise for the advocate
It is always lawful if free
questions.why: Rule 135 permits limited ordinary cards, nameplates and directory listings within its conditions, not unrestricted personal promotion.
questions.cue: Informational listing is not open-ended solicitation.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: May an advocate pay an unlicensed person to bring clients or share legal compensation with them?
wrong: Yes if the client is wealthy
questions.why: Rule 136 forbids employing or remunerating any other person to solicit professional work. Its separate restrictions address sharing compensation with an unlicensed person or assisting unauthorised practice.
questions.cue: No paid touts or unlicensed fee-sharing.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: An opposing party has counsel. May you discuss the controversy directly in counsel's absence and without consent?
wrong: Yes if you expect to win
Only if no letter is written
questions.why: Rule 137 protects represented parties from being approached behind their advocate's back about the dispute.
questions.scenario: The other side has an advocate. You want to negotiate the disputed issue directly without that advocate's presence or consent. Is that permitted?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: What should an advocate avoid concerning a contested pending matter?
questions.answer: Private merits communications behind opposing counsel's back
wrong: Serving documents on the other side
questions.why: Rule 138 also requires a copy to opposing counsel for relevant written communications, with stated exceptions.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: The client wishes to engage another advocate. What is the proper general response?
questions.answer: Respect the client's choice; address the first advocate's dues
wrong: Treat it automatically as an insult
questions.why: Rule 139 says additional assistance need not imply lack of confidence. It also addresses payment of the first advocate's dues before association.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Rule 141 permits fee division on what basis?
questions.answer: With another advocate according to agreed division of work
wrong: With a witness for favourable testimony
questions.why: The exception is tied to another advocate and actual division of work as expressed in their agreement.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Alongside courtesy, seniors are expected to be what toward junior members?
questions.why: Rule 143 pairs juniors' respect with seniors' courtesy and helpfulness. The relationship carries reciprocal responsibilities.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Can an advocate acquire an interest adverse to the client in property involved in the case?
wrong: Only if the case is delayed
questions.why: Rule 145 prevents this conflict. An advocate should not use the representation to obtain a competing personal stake.
questions.cue: Your client is not your competitor.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Before accepting employment, what does Rule 147 require disclosure of?
questions.answer: Relevant relation with the adverse party and interest in the subject matter
questions.why: The client needs to know potentially relevant relationships and interests before the advocate accepts the work.
questions.scenario: Your potential client does not know your connection with the opposing party. What must you disclose before taking the work?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Which Rule directly says an advocate shall not represent conflicting interests?
questions.why: The rule protects independent loyalty in representation. Being paid by both sides does not remove the conflict.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: What must an advocate do with client money or property?
questions.answer: Keep it separate from their own and promptly report receipt
wrong: Treat it as personal income immediately
questions.why: Rule 150 prohibits commingling and requires prompt reporting of receipt. Possession does not equal ownership.
questions.scenario: Money belonging to a client arrives in your hands. How should it be handled?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Rule 152 generally prohibits advising violation of law but preserves which advice?
questions.answer: Good-faith advice that a law is invalid
questions.why: Questioning a law's validity in good faith differs from counselling unlawful conduct. Keep that distinction clear.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: May counsel use personal belief in the client's innocence as an argument?
questions.why: Rule 156 confines advocacy to proper submissions, remedies and lawful defence. Counsel's personal assurance is not evidence.
questions.cue: Argue the case, not your personal certainty.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: An advocate is a material witness for the client, beyond merely formal matters. What should they generally do?
questions.answer: Leave the trial to other advocates
questions.why: Rule 157 separates the roles, with limited qualifications. Attestation or custody of an instrument are examples of merely formal matters.
questions.cue: Material witness? Let another advocate conduct trial.
questions.scenario: You personally witnessed a central disputed event in your client's case. Who should generally conduct the trial?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: May counsel advise a material witness to conceal themselves or avoid service?
wrong: Yes if it helps the client
questions.why: Rule 160 prohibits making material testimony unavailable in this way. Zealous representation remains within the law.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Counsel knows a cited decision was overruled. What must they avoid?
questions.answer: Citing it as valid authority without disclosing that fact
questions.why: Rule 161 also forbids intentional misquotation. Accurate treatment of authority is a duty to the court.
questions.cue: Know it is overruled? Say so.
questions.scenario: You find a helpful case but know it was overruled. What use of that decision must you avoid?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: The primary duty of a public prosecutor is what?
questions.answer: To see that justice is done
wrong: To secure conviction at any cost
questions.why: Rule 163 condemns suppression of facts or witnesses capable of showing innocence. Conviction is not the overriding goal.
questions.scenario: A prosecutor discovers evidence capable of establishing innocence. What is the prosecutor's primary duty?

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Which Rule states the general right to decline professional employment?
questions.why: Rule 171 expressly gives the right. Rule 170 instead concerns refusing cases intended merely to harass or injure. The 600-MCQ book mixes these numbers in one question.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.q: Non-observance of the Chapter XII canons is professional misconduct under which provision?
questions.why: Rule 175A addresses the canons. Rule 175B separately treats defiance of Pakistan Bar Council decisions or instructions as gross professional misconduct.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: Which Governor-General dissolved the Constituent Assembly in October 1954, leading to the Tamiz-ud-Din litigation?
questions.why: Attach the person and event to the 1955 reported case. The dispute concerned the dissolution and the legal authority used to challenge it.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: Which court initially gave Tamiz-ud-Din relief before the Federal Court proceedings?
questions.why: The historical name is Sindh Chief Court. Do not substitute a later court institution into a 1954-55 case.
questions.cue: Tamiz began in Sindh Chief Court.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: The State v Dosso is associated with which theorist's account of a successful revolution?
questions.why: The court used Kelsen's theory in treating the changed legal order as effective. This is a historical holding, not a current permission for unconstitutional action.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: Which case rejected Dosso's approach and treated Yahya Khan as a usurper?
questions.why: The 1972 case rejected the earlier validation approach. Pair the two decisions to avoid learning them as disconnected names.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: Asma Jilani sought relief concerning the detention of whom?
questions.why: The case involved detention challenges, including Asma Jilani's challenge concerning her father. This fact anchors the name to the case.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: The 1977 judgment validating Zia's takeover relied on which doctrine?
questions.why: Remember this as the reasoning of that historical decision. It should not be treated as a statement that every takeover is lawful.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: What happened to the National Assembly after the Supreme Court's decision in Nawaz Sharif v President in 1993?
wrong: It was converted into a tribunal
questions.why: The court set aside the presidential dissolution in that case. Distinguish restoration in 1993 from cases validating military takeovers.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: The 1996 Al-Jehad Trust case is principally associated with what?
questions.why: Often called the Judges' Case, it concerned the judicial appointment process. Consultation was treated as meaningful and effective, not a formality.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: In Zafar Ali Shah, what period was allowed from the October 1999 takeover for the declared objectives?
questions.why: The historical judgment specified three years from the takeover. Do not confuse it with the ordinary term of the National Assembly.

questions.subject: Cases
questions.q: Khan Asfandyar Wali v Federation is associated with constitutional scrutiny of which law?
questions.why: The case concerns the accountability framework and constitutional objections to it. It is one of the eight named cases in HEC's outline.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: Which is NOT a principal organ of the United Nations?
questions.why: The WTO is a separate organisation. The UN Charter lists six principal organs, including the ICJ.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: New UN membership is decided by the General Assembly on whose recommendation?
questions.why: Article 4 requires the Security Council's recommendation and General Assembly decision. Membership is not granted by the ICJ.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: How many members does the Security Council have?
questions.why: Five are permanent and ten are elected non-permanent members. Do not confuse total membership with permanent seats.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: The Security Council's elected non-permanent members serve for how long?
questions.why: Article 23 gives a two-year term. This differs from the ICJ judges' nine-year term.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: Important General Assembly questions generally require what majority of members present and voting?
questions.why: Article 18 distinguishes important questions from other questions. The denominator is members present and voting.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: Which Charter Article recognises individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs?
questions.why: The right is subject to the Charter's terms, including reporting measures to the Security Council. It is not an unlimited licence to use force.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: The ICJ ordinarily consists of how many judges?
questions.why: The Court has fifteen members, with no two nationals of the same state. Nine is the quorum, not the total membership.
questions.scenario: Do not confuse the minimum sitting quorum with total membership: how many judges make up the ICJ?

questions.subject: International
questions.q: An ICJ judge is elected for a term of how many years?
questions.why: Nine-year terms differ from the Court President's three-year term and the Security Council elected members' two years.

questions.subject: International
questions.q: What quorum of judges is sufficient to constitute the ICJ?
questions.why: A quorum is the minimum required to constitute the court under the provision, not its complete membership.
questions.scenario: The ICJ has fifteen members. How many judges constitute the required quorum?

questions.subject: International
questions.q: Who may be parties in contentious cases before the ICJ?
questions.why: Article 34 limits parties to states. Individuals' cases are not brought directly as contentious ICJ cases.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Salmond describes law through principles recognised and applied by the State in what?
questions.why: The administration of justice is central to this definition. Keep the author linked to the definition rather than treating all jurists' accounts as identical.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Imperative law is a rule imposed by an authority that does what?
questions.why: The defining feature is an authoritative precept or command. The source's word is authority; it need not be reduced to 'sovereign only' in every classification.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Conventional law consists of rules based on what?
questions.why: Agreement is the organising idea. Distinguish it from custom, which develops through established practice.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: A judicial remark not necessary to decide the case is called what?
questions.why: Obiter is a statement beyond the necessary basis of the decision. It may be persuasive but is different from the ratio.
questions.scenario: A judgment contains an interesting legal observation unnecessary to its outcome. Which term fits?

questions.subject: English
questions.q: What is the legal principle necessary to the court's decision commonly called?
questions.why: The ratio is the necessary legal basis of the decision. Not every sentence in a judgment has that status.
questions.scenario: You isolate the legal principle needed to reach the judgment's result. Which term fits?

questions.subject: English
questions.q: The traditional elements of possession are what?
questions.why: Corpus concerns control; animus concerns the intention associated with possession. Mens rea and actus reus belong to criminal analysis.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Which statement captures a central positivist distinction?
questions.answer: Legal validity does not necessarily depend on moral merit
wrong: Every immoral rule is automatically not law
Law and morality always mean the same thing
questions.why: The issue is identifying law, not praising it. A positivist can recognise a rule as legally valid while condemning its morality.
questions.cue: Existence of law differs from its goodness.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: The formal making of legal rules by a competent authority is called what?
questions.why: Legislation is a source of law made through an authorised lawmaking process. A stray courtroom comment is not legislation.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Bylaws made by an authorised local authority are an example of what?
questions.why: The authority acts under powers conferred by a higher legal source. Delegated lawmaking must remain within that authority.

questions.subject: English
questions.q: Jus soli identifies nationality by which connecting factor?
questions.why: Distinguish jus soli from jus sanguinis, which uses descent. This is a terminology question, not a claim that every country follows the same nationality rules.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: In the syllabus's classification, Sunnah is what kind of source?
questions.why: Sunnah is studied with the Quran among the primary textual sources. Rational techniques have a different role in derivation.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: A qualified jurist's effort to derive rules through interpretation is what?
questions.why: Ijtihad is the interpretive effort. Mujtahid is the person qualified to undertake it.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: Who is qualified to derive law directly from its sources through ijtihad?
questions.why: The term concerns the jurist's qualifications for independent derivation. It is different from following another jurist's conclusion.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: Extending a rule to a new case through a shared effective cause is what?
questions.why: Qiyas is analogy. Identify the original case, new case, rule and shared effective cause rather than merely noticing superficial similarity.
questions.scenario: A jurist extends a known rule to a new situation because both share the effective cause. What method is this?

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: Agreement of qualified jurists in the recognised sense is called what?
questions.why: Ijma concerns consensus. Qiyas concerns analogy. These are distinct routes in Islamic legal reasoning.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: The literal idea behind istihsan is to consider something what?
questions.why: Istihsan is commonly translated as juristic preference. The literal meaning is a memory aid, not a complete account of its technical operation.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: Presuming an established state continues until evidence of change is associated with what?
questions.why: Istishab reasons from continuity of an existing condition. It is different from extending a rule by analogy.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: The literal sense of fiqh is what?
questions.why: Fiqh concerns understanding of the law. The book distinguishes Shariah as law from fiqh as knowledge of it.

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: An act encouraged without a binding demand and without blame for omission is what?
questions.why: Mandub is recommended. Obligatory categories involve a binding demand, while haram is prohibited. Do not confuse encouragement with a binding obligation.
questions.scenario: An act is encouraged, but leaving it does not attract blame. Which category fits?

questions.subject: Islamic
questions.q: The ability to acquire rights and bear or perform duties is discussed under which term?
questions.why: Ahliyyah concerns legal capacity. Different aspects address acquisition of rights and valid exercise or performance.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Under the PPC, doing something with the intention of causing wrongful gain or wrongful loss is doing it how?
questions.why: Section 24 connects dishonesty to the intention of wrongful gain or loss. Actual success is not part of this definition's wording.
questions.cue: Dishonesty: wrongful gain or loss intended.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Under section 25, an act is done fraudulently when done with what?
wrong: The victim's permission in every case
questions.why: Fraudulent and dishonest are separately defined. For this definition, look specifically for intent to defraud.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: PPC section 44 includes illegally caused harm to body, mind, reputation or what?
questions.why: Injury has a wider legal meaning than a bodily wound. Harm to reputation or property can fall within the definition.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: The PPC definition requires what for a thing to be done or believed in good faith?
questions.why: Section 52 says a thing done or believed without due care and attention is not in good faith. Sincerity alone is insufficient.
questions.scenario: A person honestly believes a claim but exercised no due care or attention. What does PPC good faith require?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: The protection in section 76 concerns good-faith mistake of what?
questions.why: A person may believe themselves bound by law because they reasonably mistake the facts. Merely not knowing the law is different.
questions.cue: Mistake of fact, not ignorance of law.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Section 80 requires a lawful act, lawful manner and means, and what else?
questions.answer: Proper care and caution, without criminal intent or knowledge
wrong: An automatic immunity after any accident
questions.why: An event being called an accident is not enough. The act and manner must meet the statutory conditions.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: The section 84 test focuses on incapacity at what time?
questions.answer: At the time of doing the act
questions.why: The test concerns inability to know the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law because of unsoundness of mind at that time.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Section 96 states that an act in exercise of the right of private defence is what?
questions.why: The right has limits in the following provisions. Calling an act self-defence does not make every degree of force lawful.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: In section 299's definitions, adult means a person aged at least what?
questions.why: This is the specific Chapter XVI definition. Do not confuse it with other age tests in criminal or civil law.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Under section 299, tazir means punishment other than what?
wrong: Every sentence imposed by a judge
questions.why: The definition is by exclusion of these named categories. Tazir is punishment, not the offence itself.
questions.cue: Tazir = punishment outside those four categories.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Compensation specified in the Chapter for hurt is called what?
questions.why: Arsh is specified compensation. Daman is court-determined compensation for hurt not liable to arsh, so do not swap them.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: For qatl, when there is no wali, who has the right of qisas under section 305?
questions.why: Section 305 identifies the wali and provides for the Government where there is none. The court adjudicates; it does not become the wali merely by hearing the case.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Blocking a person from a direction in which they have a right to proceed is generally what?
questions.why: Section 339 concerns obstruction of movement in a permitted direction. Confinement adds circumscribing limits that prevent proceeding beyond them.
questions.scenario: A person unlawfully blocks a road so Bilal cannot travel in a direction he is entitled to take. What offence definition fits?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Keeping someone within circumscribing limits so they cannot proceed beyond them is what?
wrong: Only wrongful restraint with no distinction
questions.why: Section 340 defines confinement as a form of wrongful restraint within limits. Think of locking someone in a room.
questions.scenario: Bilal is unlawfully locked in a room and cannot pass beyond its limits. What offence definition fits?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Forcing or deceitfully inducing a person to go from a place is defined as what?
questions.why: Section 362 defines abduction. The concept differs from the separately defined categories of kidnapping; punishment depends on the relevant offence.
questions.cue: Force or deceit moves a person.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Dishonestly moving movable property out of another's possession without consent is what?
questions.why: Section 378 requires the relevant dishonest intention and movement for taking. Ownership and possession are not interchangeable in every problem.
questions.scenario: A person dishonestly moves another's watch from their possession without consent to take it. What offence definition fits?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Intentionally putting someone in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing delivery of property is what?
wrong: Theft by definition in every case
questions.why: Section 383 involves fear-induced delivery. Theft involves taking without consent; extortion uses fear to obtain delivery.
questions.scenario: A person intentionally threatens injury and thereby dishonestly obtains delivery of property. What offence definition fits?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: How many persons conjointly committing or attempting robbery, including those present and aiding, make dacoity?
questions.why: Section 391 counts the persons conjointly involved as specified. Do not use five as the threshold for ordinary robbery.

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: What feature is central to criminal breach of trust?
questions.answer: Entrustment or dominion followed by dishonest misuse of property
wrong: A stranger's mere glance at property
questions.why: Section 405 requires entrustment or dominion and the specified dishonest conduct. Every contractual default is not automatically this offence.
questions.scenario: Money is entrusted to a person, who then dishonestly misappropriates it. What central feature distinguishes this from a simple taking?

questions.subject: PPC
questions.q: Which concept is central to section 415 cheating?
questions.answer: Deception and the specified dishonest or harmful inducement
wrong: Only a later change of mind in every contract
questions.why: The statutory forms require deception with the relevant inducement and mental element. A mere failure to perform is not automatically cheating.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Proceedings to collect evidence conducted by police or an authorised person other than a Magistrate are called what?
questions.why: Section 4 distinguishes evidence collection by investigators from inquiry by a Magistrate or court. The role performing the process matters.
questions.scenario: Police collect evidence in the case. What name does CrPC give that process?

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Under CrPC, an inquiry is an inquiry other than a trial conducted by whom?
questions.why: The definition distinguishes inquiry from trial and from police investigation. Do not use the three words interchangeably.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: An allegation to a Magistrate seeking action under CrPC, excluding a police report, is what?
questions.why: A complaint may be oral or written and concern a known or unknown offender. The exclusion of a police report is a frequent test point.
questions.scenario: Ayesha orally alleges an offence to a Magistrate and asks for action; this is not a police report. What is it?

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: A cognizable offence is one for which police may arrest without what, under the applicable law?
questions.why: The definition links to the Schedule or another law. It does not mean police can act without legal conditions or safeguards.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Under section 59, a private person may arrest someone committing in their view what kind of offence, or a proclaimed offender?
questions.why: Both non-bailable and cognizable are required in this branch of the provision. The person must be handed over as the provision directs.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: What limit does section 50 place on restraint of an arrested person?
questions.answer: No more restraint than necessary to prevent escape
questions.why: The provision sets necessity as the measure. Arrest does not permit arbitrary extra restraint.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Without a special Magistrate's order under section 167, police detention under section 61 ordinarily cannot exceed what, excluding necessary journey time?
questions.why: Section 61 includes reasonable necessity and the twenty-four-hour ceiling. A Magistrate's remand authority is a separate matter.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Which section concerns a summons or written order to produce a document or thing for proceedings?
questions.why: Section 94 provides a production mechanism when the document or thing is considered necessary or desirable for the relevant process.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Which section concerns a search warrant for a person believed confined in circumstances amounting to an offence?
questions.why: This is a search for a person, not simply a search for stolen goods. The discovered person is brought before a Magistrate as provided.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Section 107 principally concerns security for what?
questions.why: Preventive proceedings address apprehended breach of peace under statutory conditions. They are different from conviction for a completed offence.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: A conditional order for removal of public nuisance is associated with which section?
questions.why: Section 133 provides a nuisance-removal process. Distinguish it from the urgent temporary-order mechanism of section 144.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger are principally addressed by which section?
questions.why: Section 144 is a preventive temporary-order power with legal conditions. It is not a general criminal conviction provision.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Information relating to a cognizable offence given to the officer in charge is addressed by which section?
questions.why: Oral information is reduced to writing, read over and signed as prescribed. Distinguish it from a complaint to a Magistrate.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Police generally need whose order to investigate a non-cognizable case under section 155?
questions.answer: A Magistrate with the requisite power
questions.why: Section 155(2) requires the Magistrate's order. Even then, subsection (3) excludes the power to arrest without warrant.
questions.cue: 155: Magistrate first; no automatic warrantless arrest.
questions.scenario: Police receive a non-cognizable allegation and want to investigate. Whose order do they generally need?

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: A statement to police during investigation, when reduced to writing under section 162, is generally what?
questions.answer: Not to be signed by its maker
wrong: Required to be signed like an FIR
questions.why: Do not confuse an FIR under section 154 with an investigation statement governed by section 162. Their signature rules differ.
questions.scenario: A witness gives an investigation statement to police, distinct from the FIR. What is section 162's signature rule?

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Which provision concerns recording statements and confessions by the specified Magistrate?
questions.why: The safeguards include explaining that confession is not obligatory and may be used against the maker, and examining voluntariness.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: On taking cognizance on complaint, examination of the complainant on oath, subject to exceptions, is addressed by what?
questions.why: This is a complaint route before the Magistrate. Section 204 later concerns issue of process where sufficient ground exists.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: When a person accused of a bailable offence is prepared to give bail, section 496 generally requires what?
questions.why: Bailable and non-bailable cases have different rules. Bail is not an acquittal and does not end the proceedings.
questions.scenario: A person accused of a bailable offence is ready to furnish bail. What does section 496 generally require?

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Insufficient reasonable grounds for guilt but sufficient grounds for further inquiry into a non-bailable offence engages which provision?
questions.why: The further-inquiry provision directs release on bail, or at the specified discretion on bond without sureties, pending inquiry.

questions.subject: CrPC
questions.q: Judges in a criminal appeal are equally divided. Section 429 refers the case to whom?
questions.answer: Another judge of the same court
wrong: The senior judge automatically decides alone
questions.why: The additional judge's opinion resolves the matter through the statutory procedure. Equal division does not automatically require a fresh trial.
